children: Sutanuka Ghosal Kolkata: Shares of Kalyan Jewellers, PC Jeweller and other jewellery firms on Wednesday fell by up to 4% as Bureau of Indian Standard (BIS) raised gold hallmarking fee from 45 to 75 per article. Newly-listed Lalithaa Jewellery Mart shares also hit 5% lower circuit.

The hallmarking charge has been increased from 45 to 75 per article, irrespective of its weight. This means a one-gram piece and a substantially heavier jewellery article attract the same 75 compliance charge, making the increase far more significant in percentage terms for mass-market and middle-income consumers buying lightweight jewellery. A nearly 67% hike in mandatory jewellery hallmarking charges could disproportionately raise the cost of light-weight and lower-value gold jewellery, prompting the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) to seek a review of the revised fee structure by the BIS.

BIS has revised hallmarking charges for gold and silver articles, raising the fee for gold to 75 from 45, while retaining the charge for silver at 35, with immediate effect ahead of the festive season. The increase has been notified through the BIS (Hallmarking) Amendment Regulations, 2026, dated September 14, 2026. With gold prices already at elevated levels, the industry fears that the higher fixed compliance cost could eventually be passed through the jewellery value chain, adding to the cost of every article.

GJC chairman Rajesh Rokde said the industry supports mandatory hallmarking but questioned the rationale for raising the per-article charge sharply at a time when hallmarking volumes have expanded significantly. "GJC and the jewellery industry have consistently supported hallmarking because purity assurance and consumer confidence are fundamental to our trade.

But support for hallmarking does not mean that a nearly 67% increase in the cost of mandatory compliance should pass without examination," Rokde said. "Hallmarking volumes have expanded enormously. The industry therefore deserves to understand why the per-article charge needs to rise from 45 to 75 at this stage." The council said the focus should remain on plugging leakages in the hallmarking ecosystem.

It pointed to BIS enforcement actions in Chennai, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Assam and other locations involving fake hallmarking, unauthorised operations and other instances of non-compliance. "Before increasing the burden on compliant jewellers, the priority should be to address these distortions and strengthen enforcement.

Increasing the official fee does not by itself make the hallmarking ecosystem stronger," Rokde said. GJC vice chairman Avinash Gupta said the economics of compliance needed closer examination, particularly when formal jewellers compete with unauthorised operators. "Compliance must remain commercially sustainable. If the compliant route becomes progressively more expensive while informal and unauthorised channels continue to operate, the differential between the two widens.

That is not desirable either for the Government, the industry or the consumer," Gupta said. The GJC also raised questions over discounting and commercial inducements in the hallmarking market. Gupta said the industry first needs clarity on how the existing 45 charge is actually being realised across the market before imposing a higher official fee. "If Rs 45 itself is not being uniformly realised across the market, the first question should be why that is happening and whether the present economic model requires correction.

Simply prescribing 75 without studying actual market practices may not address the underlying problem," he said. The council stressed that its demand is for a review of the fee structure and not dilution of hallmarking. The industry wants purity assurance and consumer protection to remain intact while ensuring that the cost of mandatory compliance does not disproportionately weigh on smaller-ticket jewellery purchases.

title: Jewellers' Stocks Tank on Higher Hallmarking Fees
